Orcasound · Salish Sea · 27 August 2026, 22:01 UTC

What the hydrophones actually heard

Every live Orcasound node over 6–26 August 2026, 21 calendar days and 46 node-days of audio, with a mechanical resonance at 4,816 Hz identified and rejected. It accounted for 4,161 of 12,423 detections — and for the large majority of the Southern Resident calls one node appeared to be producing.

69%of Bush Point's 1,443 Southern Resident detections were a metal object ringing, not a whale. 446 survive. The same filter removed nothing at Lab.

4,161rejected as resonance

What was run

3 hydrophones — Bush Point, North San Juan Channel, Lab — over 6–26 August 2026, 21 calendar days and 46 node-days of audio: 127,499 thirty-second windows, 1,062 hours of audio. OrcaHello, a Southern Resident presence detector, flagged 12,423 of them as holding at least one positive segment, which is 9.7% of the audio. Every one was then classified for ecotype and measured for the resonance.

  • Bush Point — Admiralty Inlet, off Whidbey Island — 48.03°N, 122.61°W — 422 h over 18 days
  • North San Juan Channel — north San Juan Channel — 48.62°N, 123.09°W — 414 h over 18 days
  • Lab — Haro Strait, west side of San Juan Island — 48.56°N, 123.17°W — 227 h over 10 days

Two counts exist and they are not the same. OrcaHello also returns a whole-window verdict, which fires on 8,780 windows; 3,643 further windows hold a positive segment without it. This page counts segments throughout, because a segment is what produces a clip to listen to.

Not included, because they are inactive in the feed registry rather than quietly missing:

  • Orcasound MaST Center — node offline upstream; acoustic signal stopped 2026-07-12, segments continued until 2026-07-17
  • Orcasound Point Robinson — hydrophone sediment-buried; the node streams but carries no usable signal

When each hydrophone heard something

Counts alone cannot tell an encounter from a fixed source. Per day they are different objects. A pod passing a node is loud for an hour and then gone; a machine is heard for a third of every day.

A named ecotype was claimed at Bush Point on 18 of its 18 recorded days, 2 to 11 hours on each — every day it was listening; North San Juan Channel on 10 of its 18 recorded days, 1 to 3 hours on each; Lab on 2 of its 10 recorded days, 1 to 2 hours on each. Southern Residents pass Admiralty Inlet roughly once a month, so a claim on every recorded day at a single node describes a fixed source rather than an animal. The embedding test below reaches the same verdict by a different route.

The 4,816 Hz resonance

Frozen Perch 2.0 embeddings put Bush Point's saturated hours in a single tight non-biological cluster, 26.3 standard deviations tighter than true background, that no other hydrophone contributed a detection to. That said the audio was not whales. It did not say what it was.

It is a high-Q mechanical resonance: a fundamental at 4,816 Hz, 20.5 dB over true background, −3 dB width 62 Hz so Q = 78, carrying integer overtones at 2× and 3× and nothing at 0.5×. Across two days its centre holds to a standard deviation of 87 Hz, 1.8%. It is struck rather than running: 15.5 dB in windows the detector fired on against 1.4 dB in windows it did not. That is a metal object near the hydrophone, moved by water, ringing at its fundamental mode.

The spectrum below is not a single line at 4,816 Hz, and the claim does not need it to be. There is further raised structure between roughly 5 and 7 kHz, one part of it higher than either marked overtone. Struck plates and bars ring in inharmonic modes as well as integer ones, so extra peaks are what a metal object should look like rather than a problem for the reading. What carries the identification is the narrowness of the 4,816 Hz peak (Q = 78), the stability of its centre across days, its integer overtones, and the absent subharmonic — not its being the only feature in the band.

A Southern Resident call is tonal with a harmonic stack in roughly 1–6 kHz, and so is this — which is why spectral flatness, centroid, band ratios and pairwise spectrum similarity all failed to separate it. The sound is not un-whale-like in its spectrum. It simply never changes, and none of those measures were measuring change.

The threshold is calibrated on this sample: 18 dB sits about 1.3 dB above the highest tone measured at the nodes where the object is absent. It is a filter for one object at one hydrophone, not a general de-noiser, and another site's contaminant will sit somewhere else in the spectrum.

Whether the numbers can be trusted

The ecotype classifier carries a measured false-positive floor on this audio: across 40 windows OrcaHello scored negative it produced 3 spurious Southern Resident calls and zero Bigg's. Every count here is tested against 7.5% for Southern Resident and against a Bigg's floor that 40 windows can only place below about 7.5%, using each hydrophone's own detections as the denominator.

Removing the resonance does not make what remains whales. It removes one identified contaminant. The false-positive floor still applies to everything left, and a no confident call verdict is weak evidence of absence rather than proof of silence.
These labels are not distinguishable from the classifier's own error rate, so they are counted but not shown as detections. Each is tested against the false-positive floor for that label using the detections at that hydrophone as the denominator, not the pooled total across all three. The highest-scoring humpback is also the quietest audio in the sample, −66.4 dB against a background median of −61.1 dB, which is what a confident label on almost no signal looks like.
  • Bush Point — humpback: 1 of 7,633 detections, 0.01%, against a floor of 0.5% (38 expected from error alone; p = 1.00).
  • Bush Point — Southern Resident: 446 of 7,633 detections, 5.84%, against a floor of 7.5% (572 expected from error alone; p = 1.00).
  • North San Juan Channel — humpback: 3 of 555 detections, 0.54%, against a floor of 0.5% (3 expected from error alone; p = 0.53).
  • North San Juan Channel — Southern Resident: 9 of 555 detections, 1.62%, against a floor of 7.5% (42 expected from error alone; p = 1.00).

Two limits on this test, both of which cut against reading it as proof. The floors are point estimates from small controls: Southern Resident is 3 of 40 windows, 95% CI 2.6%–19.9%, and Bigg's is 0 of 40, which is not a floor of zero but a floor no control this small can resolve below about 7.5% — so the Bigg's result is carried by the corroboration below and not by this test. And the test treats detections as independent draws, which a call bout is not: one encounter produces many correlated detections, which inflates any label that arrives in bouts. It is a screen, not a proof.

Does what survives hold up?

Rejecting the resonance is not the same as finding whales, so the detections that survive at Bush Point were tested separately. The tone measurement alone clears them: they sit at a median 2.7 dB over their local floor, lower than Orcasound Lab's confirmed whales at 7.8 dB.

Frozen Perch 2.0 embeddings disagree, and they are the stronger evidence because they share no training data, architecture or label space with the detector or the ecotype classifier. In embedding space the survivors sit nearest the rejected machine detections and furthest from the Lab's whales.

Mean cosine distance to the Bush Point machine cluster. Lower means more alike. Bush Point background is the control: same hydrophone, same water, same ambient noise, so if closeness to the machine were a property of the site rather than the source, it would sit as close.

Bush Point survivors240.4887

Orcasound Lab whales260.6445
The survivors are not exonerated. They sit 0.0871 closer to the machine than same-site background does, p = 0.0001 over 10,000 shuffles that exchange the two Bush Point groups (-3.9 SD of the null). The filter is necessary and not sufficient, and on this window Bush Point has no Southern Resident detection that survives scrutiny.

Only 24 survivors carry an embedding, so this is a small sample and the direction of the result matters more than its size. It also tests one alternative — the identified resonance — and cannot rule out a different contaminant.

Does the independent record agree?

A classifier agreeing with itself is not evidence. These are the days the surviving detections concentrate on, set against what people on the water recorded the same day. Nothing below was used to produce the detections.

  • Lab · Southern Resident
    29 of 30 on 2026-08-26, of which 28 fall in one 33-minute bout, 14:22–14:55 local, and 1 sits elsewhere in the day. One further detection falls on another day.
    Independently recorded that day: J and K pods, Southern Residents. “J- and K-Pods heading north towards the Strait of Georgia”, reporting “a large group of spread out whales inbound towards San Juan Island this morning”. Orcasound Lab sits on the west side of San Juan Island, on that route. — Orca Behavior Institute.
  • North San Juan Channel · Bigg's
    All 13 on 2026-08-15, in one 59-minute bout, 13:30–14:29 local.
    Independently recorded that day: nine Bigg's: T019, T019B, T019C, and six of the T049As. Two trips that day on the same two families, at 10:00 (“southwest coast of Shaw Island”, then “San Juan Channel to Spieden Island”) and at 14:00 (“San Juan Channel”, “Spieden Channel”, “Sentinel Rock”). The node listens over north San Juan Channel. — San Juan Safaris.

One non-corroboration belongs here too. A San Juan Safaris trip left Friday Harbor at 12:30 on 26 August, ran “San Juan Channel and around Henry Island into Haro Strait”, and logged a humpback with no killer whales. It does not refute the Orcasound Lab bout — that boat was working a humpback, and the pods were reported heading north — but a section listing only the confirmations would be the ranked-queue mistake again.

Limitations

  • OrcaHello gates everything downstream. 9.7% of this audio reached a classifier at all, and a Bigg's call has to sound Southern-Resident enough to trip a Southern-Resident detector.
  • The rejection threshold is one number, calibrated on 12,423 tone measurements across 21 days at three nodes, with roughly 1.3 dB of margin. It is a filter for one object at one hydrophone.
  • The false-positive floors are measured on windows OrcaHello scored negative. Those windows are quieter and less tonal than the windows a detection comes from, so the floors probably understate the rate that applies to the audio actually being labelled.
  • The same ecotype classifier recovered only 5 of 20 killer whale recordings from the Watkins database, which is expected for a model specific to Salish Sea repertoires and means absence is weakly evidenced.
  • These are the three live Orcasound nodes. MaST Center and Point Robinson are dead upstream and are listed above rather than omitted.
